## visual

### VIS-001 — Neutral surfaces, colour spent on meaning

**Rule:** Build the interface on neutral surfaces and text, and reserve saturated colour for the primary action, links, the current selection and status, keeping the brand colour to the logo and at most one chrome band.

- Why: When colour only appears where it means something, users find the next action and any problem at a glance; brand colour spread over controls competes with both.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any admin screen, including white-label or branded dashboards.
- Exceptions: Customer-facing previews (tracking page, email, storefront) render the customer's brand colours inside their own preview frame.
- Do: Gray sidebar and white cards; one blue filled "Add domain" button; a green "Active" badge in the status column.
- Don't: Brand-coloured section headers, coloured card backgrounds and coloured icons on every menu item.
- Check (static): Count distinct non-gray hues in the design tokens or compiled CSS outside the logo; at most one accent hue plus the status hues (success, warning, critical, info). No card, table or page background uses a saturated hue.
- Check (live): On a home, an index and a settings page, run a script over all visible elements reading computed color, background-color and border-color; every value with HSL saturation above 30 % belongs to the logo, the chrome band, the primary button, a link, the selected item, or a status badge or banner.

### VIS-002 — One filled primary button per view

**Rule:** Give exactly one action per view or dialog the filled accent style, and render every other action as an outlined or plain neutral button placed to its left or after it.

- Why: A single high-contrast button tells users what the page is for; two filled buttons force them to compare before acting.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Page headers, sticky save bars, dialogs and cards with actions.
- Exceptions: A view with no single main action (read-only reports, settings lists of rows) has no filled button at all. A destructive confirmation dialog uses the critical tone for its primary instead of the accent.
- Do: Header with "Buy domain" (outlined) then "Add domain" (filled accent) at the top right.
- Don't: Import, Export and Add product buttons all filled in the accent colour side by side.
- Check (static): In each page template and dialog, count buttons with the primary/filled variant (e.g. variant="primary", .btn-primary); the count is 0 or 1. Table rows contain none.
- Check (live): On each page type, run document.querySelectorAll on the primary button class (or compare computed background-color against the accent token) for visible buttons; the result length is at most 1 outside open dialogs.

### VIS-003 — Status as tinted text badges

**Rule:** Show an object's state as a small rounded badge with a text label on a light tint of its status hue, using a fixed mapping of hues to meanings (green success/active, yellow or orange warning, red critical, blue info, gray neutral or inactive).

- Why: A short label carries the meaning for everyone, the tint lets users scan a column, and a fixed mapping means the same colour never says two things.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Status columns in tables, states next to detail titles, lifecycle labels (New, Beta) and plan labels.
- Exceptions: Counts on work-queue tabs may use a neutral pill with only a number, since the tab label carries the meaning. Icon-only status is acceptable only with an accessible name and a tooltip.
- Do: "Active" in dark green text on a pale green rounded badge; "Failed" in dark red on pale red.
- Don't: A green dot with no text, or green used for "Active" on one page and for "Draft" on another.
- Check (static): Badge component accepts only a closed set of tones (e.g. success, warning, critical, info, neutral) and requires a text child; grep for raw hex or colour props passed to badges finds none. Each badge's text/background pair passes WCAG 4.5:1.
- Check (live): For every visible badge, read innerText (non-empty) and computed color/background-color; contrast is at least 4.5:1, and the same label text always renders with the same tone across pages.

### VIS-004 — Short type scale with muted secondary text

**Rule:** Use a four-step type scale (page title, section title, body, secondary) with one body size shared by labels, controls and table data, semibold headings, and a muted gray for descriptions and helper text.

- Why: A compact, predictable hierarchy keeps dense admin pages readable; muted secondary text lets labels and values lead while help stays available.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare documented)
- Applies when: All admin pages.
- Exceptions: KPI tiles and big numbers on a home page may use a larger display size for the figure itself. Marketing or empty-state illustrations are outside the scale.
- Do: 24 px semibold page title, 16 px semibold card title, 14 px regular labels and data, 13-14 px gray helper text.
- Don't: Six font sizes on one page, bold body text for emphasis, or helper text in the same colour and weight as labels.
- Check (static): Collect font-size and font-weight values from tokens or CSS; admin views use at most 5 sizes, labels, controls and table data share one size between 13 and 14 px, heading weights are 600, and no 700+ weight appears in body copy. Muted text token contrast against its background is at least 4.5:1.
- Check (live): On a settings page and an index page, read computed font-size of labels, table cells and buttons (all equal, 13-14 px) and of h1/h2 (larger, weight 600, and no section heading larger than the h1); check that helper paragraphs have a lighter colour than labels and still pass 4.5:1 contrast.

### VIS-005 — One outline icon set in text colour

**Rule:** Use a single outline icon set with one stroke weight and size per context, drawn in the surrounding text colour, and add colour to an icon only to mark the active item or a status.

- Why: Mixed icon styles and coloured icons add noise without meaning; a uniform set lets the label and the active state do the work.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Navigation, settings lists, buttons with icons and table headers.
- Exceptions: Product or integration logos and object thumbnails keep their own colours. Status icons take their status hue.
- Do: 20 px outline icons in gray-700 next to each menu label; the active item's icon switches to the accent or to full-contrast text.
- Don't: Filled icons in the sidebar, outline icons in buttons, and a different colour per menu item.
- Check (static): All icons are imported from one icon package (or one SVG sprite); icon SVGs use stroke="currentColor"/fill="currentColor" rather than hard-coded colours; sizes come from 1-2 tokens.
- Check (live): Inspect sidebar and button icons; computed color equals the parent text colour for inactive items, and only the active item or a status icon differs.

### VIS-006 — Disabled looks faded but stays in place

**Rule:** Render a disabled control at its normal size and position in a faded version of its own style, and never hide it or turn it into plain text.

- Why: Keeping it in place shows that the option exists and where it will be; the faded look says it cannot be used now, and the reason (see help-text rules) says why.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Controls unavailable because of state (no changes yet, empty list), permissions or plan.
- Exceptions: Actions the user can never get (no role or plan path leads to them) may be omitted. A locked feature may replace a whole tab with an upsell message instead of disabled controls.
- Do: A Save button at 40-50 % opacity of the accent, same width, with aria-disabled and a tooltip or nearby text explaining why.
- Don't: Removing the Save button until something changes, or graying it so far that the label is unreadable.
- Check (static): Disabled variants are derived from the enabled style (opacity between 0.4 and 0.6, or a lighter tint of the same hue), not a separate gray component, and never use display:none or visibility:hidden. Templates do not wrap unavailable actions in conditional rendering that removes them.
- Check (live): Open a form without changes and a plan- or permission-locked feature; each disabled control is in the DOM, has [disabled] or aria-disabled="true", has the same bounding-box size as its enabled state, non-empty label text, and computed opacity of at least 0.4.

### VIS-007 — Rounded corners from one scale, nested concentrically

**Rule:** Take corner radii from a small scale (control, card, pill) and give a nested element a radius equal to its container's radius minus the padding between them.

- Why: One radius scale makes components read as one system, and concentric corners keep nested shapes from looking misaligned.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare documented)
- Applies when: Cards, inputs, buttons, badges, menus and dialogs.
- Exceptions: Full-width bars (top banner, sticky save bar) and table cells stay square.
- Do: Card radius 12 px with 8 px padding around an inner input of radius 4 px; badges fully rounded.
- Don't: Cards at 4 px, buttons at 10 px, inputs at 6 px and menus at 16 px chosen ad hoc.
- Check (static): All border-radius values come from 3-4 tokens; grep the CSS for literal border-radius values outside the token file finds none. For nested rounded elements, inner radius <= outer radius minus padding.
- Check (live): Read computed border-radius of buttons, inputs, cards, badges and menus on two pages; every value belongs to the token set and the same component uses the same value everywhere.

### VIS-008 — Flat surfaces separated by one border

**Rule:** Separate surfaces with a single 1 px border or ring rather than border plus shadow, keep cards one level deep, and give sticky bars a border against scrolling content.

- Why: Stacked shadows and cards inside cards blur which layer is which; a single hairline keeps dense pages calm and makes sticky elements read as fixed.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare documented)
- Applies when: Cards, tables, sticky headers, sticky save bars and side panels.
- Exceptions: Floating layers (menus, popovers, dialogs, toasts) use a shadow to show they sit above the page. A table may sit inside a card when the card is its only container.
- Do: White card with a 1 px gray border on a light gray page; sticky save bar with a 1 px top border.
- Don't: A card with border and drop shadow containing another bordered, shadowed card.
- Check (static): Card and panel styles set either border or box-shadow, not both; no card component renders another card component as a direct descendant; sticky elements (position sticky or fixed) have a border on their content-facing edge.
- Check (live): Scroll a long settings page; the sticky bar stays visually separated by a border. Inspect cards; computed box-shadow is none (or a ring) when a border is set, and no card contains another card.

### VIS-009 — Light and dark appearance from semantic tokens

**Rule:** Define every colour as a semantic token (surface, text, muted, border, accent, status tones) and offer light and dark appearance as a personal preference that swaps those tokens.

- Why: Admin users work long sessions in varied light; semantic tokens make a dark mode a token swap instead of a second design and keep status colours meaningful in both.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Products used for long working sessions or by technical users.
- Exceptions: Customer-facing previews always render in the customer's own colours regardless of the admin appearance.
- Do: "Appearance: System / Light / Dark" in the user profile, applied instantly, stored per user.
- Don't: Hard-coded #fff backgrounds and #333 text scattered through components, or dark mode stored as an account-wide setting.
- Check (static): Components reference colour tokens only; grep for literal hex/rgb colours outside the token files finds none. A dark token set exists with values for every light token, and status pairs pass 4.5:1 in both.
- Check (live): Switch appearance to Dark in the profile; on a home, an index and a settings page the body background is dark (relative luminance below 0.2), every visible text and badge pair passes 4.5:1, the choice survives a reload, and another user's session stays on its own setting.

### VIS-010 — User-selectable row density on work queues

**Rule:** On tables people process all day, let each user choose between a compact and a comfortable row density, and keep the choice per user.

- Why: Power users want more rows on screen while occasional users need room to read; a per-user density setting serves both without changing the default layout.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Work-queue tables with many rows handled repeatedly (orders, tickets, shipments).
- Exceptions: Occasional lists and settings pages keep one fixed density (see the layout rule on constant density).
- Do: "Row density: Compact / Comfortable" in the table settings menu, remembered for that user.
- Don't: Changing row height between sections of the same page, or one global density switch that also shrinks forms.
- Check (static): The work-queue table component takes a density prop bound to a stored user preference; row height values come from two spacing tokens.
- Check (live): Switch density on the work-queue table; row height changes, other pages stay unchanged, and the choice persists after reload and on the next login.

## layout

### LAY-001 — Width set by page type

**Rule:** Constrain settings and form pages to a centred content column with a max width of roughly 640 to 1040 px, and let index, log and dashboard pages use the full content width.

- Why: Short forms and explanatory text become hard to scan when lines and label-to-control distances stretch across a wide screen, while tables need every pixel for columns.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Settings pages, create/edit forms and single-object configuration pages viewed on screens wider than about 1100 px.
- Exceptions: Index tables, logs, analytics and dashboards use full or large width. A settings page whose main content is a wide table may widen to the large width. One reference keeps settings full width with no cap; the other two cap the column (about 785 px and about 1024 px at a 1440 viewport), and the public layout guidance documents a small width for focused forms.
- Do: Settings content in a centred column with max-width 960px; the orders table on the next page spans the full main area.
- Don't: A three-field settings form stretched to 1800 px, with the label on the far left and the control on the far right.
- Check (static): The settings/form page container declares a max-width between 640px and 1040px and is centred (margin-inline auto or a centred grid track); the index page container has no max-width, or one of at least 1200px.
- Check (live): At a 1440x900 viewport, on a settings page, getBoundingClientRect() of the main content column has width <= 1040 and its left and right gaps inside the main area differ by less than 24px; on an index page, the table width is at least 90% of the main area width.

### LAY-002 — Full-width index tables

**Rule:** Let list and index tables span the full width of the main content area, with the page header and toolbar aligned to the same edges.

- Why: Index pages are scanned across many columns; a capped width forces horizontal scrolling or hidden columns long before the screen runs out.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any page whose main content is a table or list of records.
- Exceptions: Empty states and promotional placeholders on an index route may sit in a narrower centred card.
- Do: Title, toolbar and table share the same left and right edges and fill the main area.
- Don't: A 900 px wide table centred on a 1440 px screen with the last three columns behind a horizontal scrollbar.
- Check (static): The index page wrapper sets no max-width below 1200px; the table element or its wrapper has width 100% of the main area.
- Check (live): At 1440x900, the table's left and right edges are within 4px of the toolbar's and page header's edges, and for a table with 8 or fewer columns, its scroll container has scrollWidth <= clientWidth.

### LAY-003 — Annotated settings sections

**Rule:** On wide settings pages, put each section's title and description in a narrow left column and its controls in a wider right column; stack the description above the controls when the column is narrow.

- Why: Users read what a group of settings does before touching it, and a fixed left gutter of explanations makes a long settings page scannable by topic.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify documented, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Settings pages made of several sections where each section needs one or two sentences of explanation, and the content column is at least about 800 px wide.
- Exceptions: When the settings column is capped below about 800 px, use a single column with the heading and description above the controls (the reference that dropped the annotated layout also uses the narrowest column). List-style settings pages whose content is a table of items (couriers, members, keys) skip the annotation. A row-level variant is fine, with one setting per row, its text on the left and its switch or button on the right (one reference uses only this variant).
- Do: Section card with "Packaging" and a two-line description in the left third, the fields in the right two thirds.
- Don't: Descriptions placed in tooltips, or a description below the last field where nobody reads it.
- Check (static): Each settings section is a two-track grid (for example grid-template-columns 1fr 2fr) with a heading plus description element in the first track and form controls in the second, collapsing to one track below the breakpoint.
- Check (live): At 1440x900, for each settings section, the heading's right edge is left of the first control's left edge and the description's top is within 24px of the first control's top; at 390 px wide, the description sits above the controls with no overlap.

### LAY-004 — Two-column object detail

**Rule:** Lay out object detail and edit pages in two columns, a main work column of about two thirds and a side column of about one third for status, summary and metadata.

- Why: Keeping status, tags and key facts in a fixed side column lets users edit the main content without losing sight of the object's state.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: An object has one main editable body (items, description, addresses) plus short metadata (status, owner, tags, notes, summary totals).
- Exceptions: Objects made of several independent areas of equal weight (overview, metrics, settings, logs) use tabs on a single full-width column instead; one reference does this on every detail page. A side column may also hold an in-page table of contents for long settings pages.
- Do: Main column with line items and timeline; side column with status, customer, tags and notes.
- Don't: Status and tags at the bottom of a long single column, or a side column that holds the primary editable content.
- Check (static): The detail template defines a main region and an aside/complementary region with roughly a 2:1 width ratio (for example grid-template-columns 2fr 1fr), and status/metadata components render in the aside.
- Check (live): At 1440x900, the page has an element with role complementary (or aside) whose width is 25-40% of the main area, placed right of the main column, and it contains the status badge or metadata; at 390 px wide it stacks below or above the main column.

### LAY-005 — Stack of titled sections

**Rule:** Build settings and long forms as a single vertical stack of titled sections or cards, one topic per section, and never nest cards inside cards.

- Why: Sections give long pages a scannable rhythm and a place for each topic's description; nested card layers add borders without adding structure.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any settings page or form with more than about five inputs.
- Exceptions: A table inside a section (for example a list of certificates) is fine; it is not a nested card. Very short pages with one or two controls may skip the card.
- Do: Five cards titled Store details, Address, Currency, Time zone, Order IDs, each with its own heading and short description.
- Don't: Twenty fields in one card, or a card containing three bordered sub-cards.
- Check (static): Forms with more than 5 inputs are split into section/card components each with an h2 or h3; no card component renders another card component as a direct or nested child.
- Check (live): On a settings page with more than 5 inputs, every input, select, textarea and role=switch control sits inside a section or card that has its own h2 or h3, and no element with the card class or role has a descendant with the same card class or role.

### LAY-006 — One spacing scale, constant density

**Rule:** Use a single spacing scale built on a 4 px base and keep the same density from the top to the bottom of a page.

- Why: A shared scale keeps alignment consistent across pages built by different people, and density changes mid-page make sections look unrelated.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: All pages.
- Exceptions: Data-heavy tables may use a denser row height than forms, as long as the whole table uses the same one. Product-wide density levels differ between the references (medium vs high), so pick one level per product and keep it.
- Do: Gaps of 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32 px only; every card on the page uses the same 16 px padding.
- Don't: Cards with 13 px and 22 px padding on the same page, or a compact table followed by a spacious form section with no reason.
- Check (static): Spacing values in CSS or design tokens are all multiples of 4px (grep margin, padding, gap values); cards on one template share one padding token.
- Check (live): Collect computed padding, margin and gap of all elements in main; at least 95% of non-zero values are multiples of 4px, and all sibling cards report the same padding.

### LAY-007 — Side panels reflow content

**Rule:** Dock assistant and inspector panels on the right edge and reflow the main content to the remaining width instead of overlaying it.

- Why: Users keep working on the page while the panel is open; an overlay hides the very content the panel is talking about.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: A persistent side panel (AI assistant, help, inspector) that the user keeps open while working, at viewports of about 1024 px and wider.
- Exceptions: Below about 1024 px the panel may cover the content as a full-height sheet with a close control. Short confirmation dialogs remain modal.
- Do: Opening the assistant narrows the main column to about two thirds and the table re-flows.
- Don't: A panel that slides over the right third of the page and hides the Save button.
- Check (static): The panel is a sibling of main in the layout grid/flex container (not position fixed over it), and opening it changes the main region's width.
- Check (live): At 1440x900, record main's width, open the panel, and confirm main's width shrank by roughly the panel width and no part of main sits under the panel (elementFromPoint at main's right edge returns an element inside main).

### LAY-008 — Content owns the phone width

**Rule:** At phone width, give the main content the full viewport width by stacking columns into one and moving persistent chrome out of the way.

- Why: On a 390 px screen any rail or side column that stays open squeezes forms and tables into an unusable strip.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Viewports narrower than about 768 px.
- Exceptions: Tables with many columns may scroll horizontally inside their own container, or render as a list of records; the page itself must not scroll horizontally.
- Do: At 390 px the sidebar becomes a menu button, the detail side column stacks under the main column, and the table becomes a list.
- Don't: A settings sidebar that stays expanded at 390 px and leaves 150 px for the form.
- Check (static): Multi-column layout grids switch to a single track below a breakpoint of about 768px; no fixed-width rail or aside is rendered unconditionally at that width.
- Check (live): At 390x844, document.documentElement.scrollWidth <= window.innerWidth, and the main content region's width is at least 90% of the viewport width.
